title.en: The disappointing worlds of Adam and Noach

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Bereishis and Noach a world that was spoiled: Adam ate from the tree, later generations sinned, and the flood came. He brings Noach's mention in the Rosh Hashanah zichronos and explains that Noach and the animals that kept their own species were saved to start a new world.

title.en: Creation is in man's hands

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem handed creation to man, so each person's share of the world depends on his deeds, as the fruit of Eretz Yisrael grew huge when the Jews kept the Torah. The flood generation sinned so much that even animals and the earth were corrupted, while Noach's share, including Eretz Yisrael, stayed pure.

title.en: The plan after the flood fails

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that three sinned in the ark, Cham, the dog and the raven, so the plan for a world of tzaddikim was shattered. He asks how one can say Hashem was disappointed, citing 'vayinachem', and explains that the world's inhabitants did not keep the condition on which they were saved.

title.en: Avraham and the tikkun of the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that with Avraham the world of tikkun begins: the Jewish people, through history and exile, slowly repair the world, as the nations learn from them and come to the foundations of the Torah, until Moshiach. He then begins the parsha's account of Avraham going down to Egypt and Pharaoh taking Sarah.

title.en: The Ramban's charge and the Zohar's defense

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that Avraham committed a great sin, going to Egypt and not protecting Sarah, which caused the Egyptian exile. He explains that the Ramban had the Zohar, which defends Avraham: he knew that Sarah's purity in Pharaoh's house would protect all Jewish women in Egypt, as Yosef's restraint protected the men.

title.en: The Torah tells what will happen

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Avraham's story opens with a sin, and compares the beginning of Shemos, where Moshe's parents are not named. He explains that Hashem runs the world with a plan, that the Torah, unlike other history books, tells what will happen, as Haazinu foretells the whole destiny of the Jewish people, and brings the Ramban's argument from the fulfillment of Haazinu that the end, Moshiach, must come too.

title.en: Why Avraham gets no introduction

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal that the Torah hides who Moshe's parents were because Moshe had to be born regardless of their merits. In the same way, the Torah introduces Noach as a tzaddik but begins Avraham's story only with 'lech lecha', leaving out his self-sacrifice in Ur Kasdim, because the Jewish people had to come, as Chazal read 'b'hibaram' as 'b'Avraham'.

title.en: Redemption comes regardless

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Ramban stresses Avraham's sin to show that Avraham had to come regardless, for the Jewish people must bring the world to its tikkun. He brings the Ramban at the end of Haazinu that the redemption will come at its time even without teshuvah, and applies it to every Jew, who must in the end reach his tikkun, since no one will be cast away.

title.en: Lot captured for the spark of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the four kings went to war to capture Lot of all people, and answers that Moshiach was to come from Lot through Moav and Rus, which the kings, as sorcerers, knew; Avraham went to war to ensure Moshiach would come. He adds that the four kings are the four exiles, the last being Edom, the 'king of nations' of today's Western society.

title.en: Esav bites with a kiss

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the explanation that when Esav kissed Yaakov he really wanted to bite him, and when he could not bite, he 'bit' with a kiss. He applies this to the exile of Edom, which once persecuted the Jews and now draws them in through friendship and intermarriage, and warns the young men in yeshiva to strengthen themselves before they go out into the world.

catalogTitle: אברהם אבינו זכה למערת המכפלה ע"י גודל מדת החסד שלו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham Avinu won the Me'aras HaMachpelah through his self-sacrificing chesed, and that a person who devotes himself to others gains the power of the prayer of the many, which the Jewish people sorely need in a time of danger and talk of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash that Adam and Chava refused to have Avraham and Sarah buried beside them, and explains that they owned the cave and had a fair claim to their privacy. Avraham overcame that claim through his hospitality three days after his bris: one who ignores his own comfort for others earns that others ignore theirs for him, and he took Adam 'by the hand', the hand being chesed. From Avraham, who brought people under the wings of the Shechinah, the Mashgiach moves to 'Shall I hide from Avraham': with the Parashas Derachim and the Gemara in Rosh Hashanah he explains that one who is mezakeh rabim has the prayer of the many, which helps even after a decree. He calls on listeners to weigh their careers by this, and to pray now. He then speaks of the danger to the Jewish people, the harm when nations talk about Jews, the need for Torah as a wall, the folly of fixing dates for Moshiach, and ends with preparing for Moshiach now.

en: According to the Mashgiach, Adam and Chava owned the Me'aras HaMachpelah and by the law of fairness could keep Avraham and Sarah out to preserve their own privacy.
Avraham's hospitality while in pain after his bris changed the reckoning: one who disregards his own comfort for guests must be received the same way, so Adam and Chava lost their claim.

The Mashgiach explains that Avraham's hospitality was a means to bring people under the wings of the Shechinah, and he says every Jew who learns the parsha must ask himself whether he works to bring others close.

One who is mezakeh rabim has the status of the many, so his prayer is the prayer of the many and can help even after a decree has been sealed; this is why Hashem revealed the fate of Sedom to Avraham.
The Mashgiach says the Jewish people now need prayers, and every person should plan his future so as to be among those who bring others close and whose prayer counts as the prayer of the many.
It is harmful when the nations talk about the Jews; the Mashgiach says the Jewish people's protection is Torah and tefillah, the 'wall' of the passuk.
The Mashgiach warns that no one can know the end of days: calculations of the end are only signs to awaken teshuvah, and declaring that Moshiach must come at a given time is heresy.

candidateTopics: prayer of the many after a decree

title.en: The calf that led Avraham to the cave

summary.en: The Mashgiach retells the Midrash on 'and to the cattle Avraham ran': the calf fled into the Me'aras HaMachpelah, where Avraham saw Adam and Chava and longed for the place as a burial site. He brings the hint that 'bakar' has the letters of 'kever'.

title.en: Adam and Chava's claim to the cave

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Adam and Chava wanted to leave rather than lie beside Avraham and Sarah, until Avraham took Adam by the hand. He explains that the cave belonged to them, comparing the halachos of fairness such as damage by sight, so they had a right to keep the newcomers out.

title.en: Hospitality that overrode their claim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham's hospitality at ninety-nine, in pain after his bris, changed the law of fairness: one who ignores his own discomfort for guests must be received without regard for others' comfort. He adds that 'hand' in Chazal means chesed, so Avraham won Adam over with his chesed.

title.en: Hospitality to bring people under the Shechinah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Avraham's hospitality taught guests to thank the Ribono shel Olam, and that he himself knew what it means to come under the wings of the Shechinah. He says every Jew learning the parsha must ask whether his own life is directed toward bringing others close.

title.en: Why Hashem revealed Sedom to Avraham

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what 'Avraham will become a great nation' has to do with revealing Sedom's fate. He brings the Parashas Derachim on Moshe's plea 'You have begun', the Gemara in Taanis that Moshe was needed by the many, and the Gemara in Rosh Hashanah that the prayer of the many helps even after a decree; Avraham, who would leave behind a people serving Hashem, had the status of the many.

title.en: The prayer of one who serves the many

summary.en: The Mashgiach draws the lesson that whoever devotes himself to others, even when he davens alone, has the power of the prayer of the many. He says the Jewish people now need prayers, that events should be read as signs from heaven, and that each person should plan his future to be among those who bring others close.

title.en: Giving up comfort for the Jewish people

summary.en: The Mashgiach clarifies that a bachur in yeshiva should not leave his learning, but one choosing a path in life should aim to raise a people that serves Hashem. Pointing to soldiers who give their lives, he asks why one would not give up some luxuries to serve the Jewish people, and calls those who learn and daven truly the real soldiers.

title.en: Prayers kept in reserve

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a pshat he heard in the name of the Yitav Lev: in an emergency there is no time to daven, so prayers must be ready beforehand, and Avraham's prayer for Sedom, which did not help, was stored for his descendants. He adds that this parsha holds the Rosh Hashanah reading and that Avraham's time was one of Nisan and chesed, a time to arouse mercy.

title.en: A little sister: when nations speak of Israel

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the political situation as a sign from heaven to arouse mercy, with the danger growing. He explains 'we have a little sister' as the Jewish people lacking leaders to nourish them, and 'on the day she is spoken of' as the danger when nations talk about Jews, bringing Rashi on Yosef and the butler.

title.en: A goy remains a goy; Torah is the wall

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the world now talks only of the Jews and blames them for its discomforts, recalling how Jews were blamed for plagues, and argues from Germany that there is no such thing as progress in the nations. With 'go my people, enter your rooms' he warns against mixing with the nations, and with 'if she is a wall' he says Torah and tefillah are the Jews' protection, to be accepted upon oneself now.

title.en: Signs of Moshiach and the danger of dates

summary.en: The Mashgiach says tzaddikim felt Moshiach was close, and speaks of a comet that people linked to a Zohar about a star before Moshiach's coming. He warns that past dates set for the end brought great dangers instead, and brings the Gemara in Megillah on the miscounted seventy years and Daniel, who did not understand his own calculations.

title.en: No one knows the reckoning of the end

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of people who sold their businesses expecting Moshiach, and of a tzaddik who feared that a failed date would shake people's emunah. He concludes that hints of Moshiach in the sefarim are only possible times, that saying he must come then is heresy, and that the signs should spur teshuvah, Torah, tzedakah and tefillah.

title.en: The Bluzhever Rav and the hidden heichal

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads from the sefer Divrei Emunah a story of a Jew whose children were killed in a time of massacres, who asked the Bluzhever Rav to seek a heavenly answer through fasts. The Bluzhever Rav answered that even the great ones of the past would know no more now, for the matter is hidden above. The Mashgiach concludes that the time of the end is Hashem's private matter and the Gemara's signs are only signs.

title.en: The tzaddikim's reckonings and Eretz Yisroel's rescue

summary.en: The Mashgiach rejects the claim that the tzaddikim who did not send their followers to Eretz Yisroel were at fault, saying they had Torah reckonings and Eretz Yisroel was not safer. He tells how, when Rommel's army reached its borders, three tzaddikim went with a Sefer Torah to the kever of the Ohr HaChaim and returned assured that the Jews there would be saved, and the army was pushed back.

title.en: Hashem's plan and preparing for Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ohr HaChaim that the people of Sedom were souls of the generation of the dispersion, and with the example of Yaakov going down to Mitzrayim explains that Hashem has reckonings beyond us and His plan is carried out. He closes that when Moshiach comes each Jew will be received according to how he prepared, and the time to prepare with Torah and avodah is now.

catalogTitle: The Differences Between the מסירת נפש of אברהם אבינו by the עקידה and להבדיל Today's Suicide Bomber

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham's mesiras nefesh at the Akeidah differs from the self-sacrifice of nations and of today's suicide bombers, because a Jew's love for Hashem is inborn and intrinsic, shown by the simcha and calm with which Avraham and Yitzchak went.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by explaining that each Shabbos is woven from its sedra and never repeats, and that the events of the parsha recur spiritually: as Hashem visited Avraham after his milah, He visits our sick generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha. He tells how the Belzer Rav had a cheder learn the current sedra so a frozen river would thaw. Shabbos Vayera holds both Rosh Hashanah readings and is a miniature Rosh Hashanah. He then asks what is special about the Akeidah when nations and suicide bombers also give their lives, and answers that Avraham and Yitzchak went with simcha and calm. Through the dispute of Yitzchak and Yishmael over milah, the Rambam on coerced consent, and milah versus tefillin, he shows that a Jew is a Jew from birth. A Jew's love for Hashem is intrinsic, like a parent's love for a child, unlike the indoctrinated devotion of terrorists.

en: Every Shabbos is woven from its sedra, has its own unique task, and never repeats itself.
Shabbos Vayera contains the Torah readings of both days of Rosh Hashanah and is therefore a miniature Rosh Hashanah.
The uniqueness of the Akeidah was not the readiness to give a son, which nations have also shown, but that Avraham and Yitzchak went with simcha and without any nervousness.
A Jew is a Jew from birth, independent of his understanding and choice, which is why milah is done at eight days while tefillin waits for bar mitzvah.
A Jew's love for Hashem is an intrinsic love, like a parent's love for a child, because Jews are a part of Hashem and His children.

title.en: Every Shabbos is woven from its sedra

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each Shabbos is made of the fabric of its sedra and never repeats. He counts 600,000 Shabbosos in the world's history, matching the 600,000 souls of Israel and the 600,000 letters of the Torah, and shows how letters are made of smaller letters.

title.en: Hashem visits our sick generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the oneg of Shabbos should be joy with Hashem, and that what the sedra tells repeats itself spiritually: as Hashem visited Avraham on the third day after his milah, He visits us this Shabbos. He describes our generation as very sick, with intermarriage, the internet and cell phones, because the Satan fights the approach of Moshiach in ikvesa d'Meshicha.

title.en: The Belzer Rav and the frozen river

summary.en: The Mashgiach names the Akeidah as the pinnacle of the parsha and says the tzaddikim taught to live with the parsha. He tells how lumber merchants came to the Belzer Rav when the river stayed frozen, and he traced it to the cheder learning Mikeitz instead of the current sedra; once they switched, the ice melted.

title.en: Shabbos Vayera as a miniature Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that both Rosh Hashanah readings, the remembering of Sarah and the Akeidah, are in this sedra, so this Shabbos is a small Rosh Hashanah in which one can complete what was lacking. He adds that the shofar comes from the ram of the Akeidah and that the Akeidah is mentioned in Rosh Hashanah prayers and said every morning.

title.en: What made the Akeidah special: simcha

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what is special about Avraham's readiness to sacrifice Yitzchak, when nations also did such things and soldiers give their lives for a cause. He answers that Avraham went with simcha, walked at Yitzchak's pace, and came home as if nothing special had happened, while suicide bombers are visibly nervous and often give up; he contrasts the toll in Iraq with Hashem's protection in Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Yitzchak, Yishmael and the age of milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what pride there is in the Akeidah if Yishmael's descendants also give their lives. He brings Rashi on the dispute in which Yishmael boasted of consenting to milah at thirteen and Yitzchak answered he would give all his limbs, and asks why Hashem gave a Jewish boy the greatest mitzvah at eight days, denying him the chance to show devotion.

title.en: A Jew is born a Jew: milah and tefillin

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that a Jew's milah shows that he is a Jew from birth. He brings the Rambam on how forced consent counts, since every Jew truly wants to do Hashem's will and only the body resists, and the Gemara that calls both milah and tefillin a sign: milah at eight days shows Jewishness without daas, tefillin at bar mitzvah reflects choice, and Yishmael has only that kind of devotion.

title.en: Intrinsic love versus indoctrination

summary.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes love based on reasons from intrinsic love, like a mother's love for her child or a person's love for himself. A Jew's love for Hashem is intrinsic, since every Jew is a part of Hashem and His child, which is why whole communities gave their lives in the Crusades without exception; the Arabs, by contrast, are trained and indoctrinated in camps, like soldiers in an army. The recording ends mid-thought.

catalogTitle: ביאור השבח לה' כשאנו אומרים - אלקי אברהם

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that saying 'Elokei Avraham' in Shemoneh Esrei is a praise of Hashem because Hashem's chesed was revealed through Avraham, whose mesirus nefesh for chesed, and finally against his own nature at the Akeidah, fills Parshas Vayera.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rabbeinu Bachya: the people of Sedom were reincarnations of the generation of the Tower of Bavel, and those of Tzoar, spared by Lot's prayer, came back again as Korach's congregation. From here he speaks of hidden accounts from earlier lives behind terrible decrees, and brings the Chasam Sofer on Yirmiyahu and Chanamel's field: Yirmiyahu was a reincarnation of Shlomo HaMelech, yet Hashem, 'G-d of all flesh', does not punish the new body. The Mashgiach asks how tikkun then works, and distinguishes the soul's repair from the body's suffering. He then turns to his main theme: the first bracha of Shemoneh Esrei praises Hashem as 'Elokei Avraham' because Avraham revealed Hashem's chesed, with mesirus nefesh, even toward idolaters and the cruel people of Sedom. He brings the Lubliner Rav, Onkelos, the Bnei Yissaschar and the Ran on Yishmael's expulsion and the Akeidah, and ends that every Jew carries a piece of Avraham and Yitzchak.

en: According to Rabbeinu Bachya, the people of Sedom were the generation of the Tower of Bavel reincarnated, and the people of Tzoar, who escaped through Lot's prayer, returned as Korach's congregation to complete their tikkun.

The Chasam Sofer explains that Yirmiyahu was a reincarnation of Shlomo HaMelech, and Hashem's answer 'I am Hashem, G-d of all flesh' teaches that the new body, which did not sin, is not punished for the soul's earlier sin.
The praise in 'Elokei Avraham' is that Hashem's attribute of chesed was revealed in the world through Avraham, so a person can only say it properly after toiling in the parshiyos of the Avos.
Avraham's chesed was mesirus nefesh: he served idol-worshipping Arabs three days after his milah and prayed for Sedom, people who despised chesed and opposed him.
To merit chesed beyond nature one must do chesed with mesirus nefesh beyond nature, which is how Avraham explained his request of Sarah, and soon afterward Sarah was remembered.
Sending away Yishmael and the Akeidah were tests that required Avraham, the man of chesed, to act against his own nature, and according to the Ran the Akeidah was only a request, not a command.
Every Jew has a piece of Avraham and of Yitzchak, and in each small struggle with his will he can awaken that point of mesirus nefesh.

candidateTopics: the akeidah as a test against nature

title.en: Sedom, the Tower generation and Korach

summary.en: The Mashgiach continues with Rabbeinu Bachya on the sedra and brings his teaching that the people of Sedom were reincarnations of the generation of the Tower of Bavel, who came again as Korach's congregation. Using the Targum on the kings in Lech Lecha, he explains that Tzoar, spared by Lot's prayer, still needed its punishment later.

title.en: Hidden accounts behind terrible decrees

summary.en: Applying this, the Mashgiach addresses those who ask why righteous Jews and their children perished in the Holocaust and in earlier decrees, saying Hashem has accounts we do not know that will become clear when Moshiach comes. He cites sefarim that the victims of the gezeiros of Tach were the zealots of the Second Temple who opposed Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.

title.en: Yirmiyahu buys Chanamel's field

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer on the haftarah of Yirmiyahu chapter 32: just before the churban Hashem had Yirmiyahu buy his cousin Chanamel's field as a sign that fields would again be bought in Eretz Yisroel. He explains Chanamel's own plan: by selling to a tzaddik in a sale of the land now and the produce later, he hoped to keep a share that the conquerors could not take.

title.en: Yirmiyahu as Shlomo's reincarnation

summary.en: Continuing the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach explains that Yirmiyahu was a reincarnation of Shlomo HaMelech, whose marriage to Pharaoh's daughter on the night of the Temple's dedication brought the decree of churban, so Yirmiyahu feared Chanamel's security was false. Hashem's reply, 'I am Hashem, G-d of all flesh', means the new body did not sin and is not punished.

title.en: Tikkun of the soul and the luz bone

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks: if the new body is innocent, what is the point of returning for tikkun? He answers that an old blemish must still be repaired, but a tzaddik's body does not suffer for it, and after teshuvah one is a new person. He adds that the luz bone did not benefit from Adam's sin, and connects it to melave malka and to the tzaddikim mentioned on motzaei Shabbos.

title.en: Why 'Elokei Avraham' is a praise

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the parshiyos of the Avos must be toiled over like a Tosafos, because the first bracha of Shemoneh Esrei, 'Elokei Avraham', is a praise and even serves as its malchus. Hashem is a Rav Chesed, and this was revealed through Avraham, who hated idolatry with a depth beyond our five chapters of Avodah Zarah, yet served idol-worshipping Arabs three days after his milah.

title.en: The cruelty of Sedom and Avraham's prayer

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells Chazal's account of the girl in Sedom who secretly fed a poor man and was smeared with honey and killed by bees, and explains Sedom's outlook that the poor are parasites to be wiped out. Avraham nevertheless prayed for them, even speaking sharply toward Heaven, and this mesirus nefesh for chesed shows how great is Hashem's chesed, the praise in 'Elokei Avraham'.

title.en: Lot's descendants, the angels and Onkelos

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Ammon and Moav, though from Lot of Avraham's family, kept Sedom's point of no chesed, and brings the Ramban that Sedom was judged because it was in Eretz Yisroel. He brings that the three angels came from milah, priah and metzitzah, then the Lubliner Rav on 'when Elokim made me wander from my father's house': Avraham spoke to Sarah of Hashem's chesed in saving him from idolatry, which Onkelos, himself a convert, understood.

title.en: Chesed beyond nature and Sarah's laughter

summary.en: On 'this is your kindness', the Mashgiach explains that to receive chesed beyond nature one must do chesed with mesirus nefesh, citing the Bnei Yissaschar, and this is how Avraham explained to Avimelech why he asked Sarah to say she was his sister. Sarah was then remembered, and the Mashgiach brings the Midrash that many barren women and prayers were answered with her, though not everyone recognized it was in her merit.

title.en: Yishmael's expulsion and the Akeidah: against his nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that both Rosh Hashanah readings come from this parsha, which speaks of answered prayers. He then explains that sending Yishmael away early in the morning was, like the Akeidah, a test against Avraham's nature of chesed, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar that at the Akeidah Yitzchak took on love while Avraham took on Yitzchak's gevurah.

title.en: The Ran on the Akeidah and a piece of Avraham

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Derashos HaRan that the Akeidah was only a request, as Rashi reads 'na', so the test was to act against chesed when it was only a measure of piety. He closes that every Jew carries a piece of Avraham and Yitzchak, can awaken mesirus nefesh in small struggles, and must toil in this sedra to say 'Elokei Avraham' properly.

catalogTitle: התורה היא תורת חיים - הקריאה של ראש השנה מעורר הזמן

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah is a Torah of life, so that a Jew who learns Vayera, the Rosh Hashanah reading, lives through the Akeidah with Avraham, and he draws from it that the time until Chanukah is a renewed Rosh Hashanah in which a generation without feeling must serve Hashem with simple routine.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the idea that the reading of each week awakens its time, illustrated by the Belzer Rav's advice to timber merchants and by Chazal's account of Rebbi and Nevuchadnetzar. Learning Vayera, a Jew lives through the Akeidah with Avraham and accepts mesirus nefesh. From Avraham and Sarah's long wait he turns to the hope for Moshiach, citing the Imrei Noam and the Rimanover that a year when Shabbos falls on Erev Pesach is auspicious, along with other signs of the year and the war between Iran and Iraq read through a Pesikta. He then explains the custom of the Ba'al Shem Tov's students to wish a gmar chasimah until Chanukah: each later, weaker generation was shown a further chance, ending with simple routine. He applies this to a young man's first twenty years and closes with the Akeidah seen from afar, avodah without feeling in a time of hester panim.

en: The reading of the week is connected to everything that happens in that week; one lives through the events of the parsha rather than hearing old stories.
Since every Jew was included in Avraham, he lives through the Akeidah when he learns Vayera, and it is a time to accept mesirus nefesh for every test.
Some times are more auspicious for the redemption, and then each Jew must exert himself more in Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.
The students of the Ba'al Shem Tov wish a gmar chasimah until Chanukah, because each later generation was shown another chance: Hoshana Rabbah, then Chanukah.
The first twenty years of a person's life are his period until Chanukah, a time to build mind and heart before the seal.
The Akeidah was a test of serving Hashem from afar, without feeling, which corresponds to the last generation before Moshiach.

candidateTopics: youth as a time of preparation

title.en: The weekly reading and the frozen river in Belz

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens: Vayera carries the Rosh Hashanah reading, the Torah is a Torah of life, and every Shabbos is woven from the pesukim of its parsha. He tells how Rabbi Shalom of Belz told timber merchants that their logs were stuck in a frozen river because their children were learning Mikeitz in Nissan, and that learning the week's parsha would free the river.

title.en: Rebbi and Nevuchadnetzar; living through the Akeidah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from Chazal that Rebbi did not curse Nevuchadnetzar while learning a passage where he was still alive, but did when reading the Megillah, because one who learns is truly in that time. So a Jew learning Vayera lives through the Akeidah with Avraham, of whom he was a part, and should accept mesirus nefesh for every test, large and small.

title.en: "Hashem remembered Sarah": waiting for the promise

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one must draw from the parsha the emunah that Hashem helps even after a long wait: Avraham and Sarah waited many years, and Klal Yisrael, whom Sarah hints at, waits for the promise sworn after the Akeidah. He compares the coming of Moshiach to a birth with its pangs, and says some times are more auspicious, when one must strike while the iron is hot.

title.en: A year when Shabbos falls on Erev Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Imrei Noam of Zhikov on Pekudei, citing the Rimanover, that a year when Shabbos is Erev Pesach is auspicious for the redemption, with proofs from the entry into Eretz Yisrael and the erection of the Mishkan. Since this year is such a year, and Moshiach can come either at its fixed time or earlier through merit, each Jew must exert himself more.

title.en: The thinning partition and the signs of this year

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that the closer it comes to Moshiach, the less is asked and the more suffering has accumulated. He brings the Satmar Rav's answer why the shofar frightens the Satan anew each year: the partition holding back Moshiach grows thinner. He lists this year's signs: the year after shmitah, Birkas Hachamah in Nissan, two Adars hinting at the erasing of Amalek, and a three-day Purim in Yerushalayim.

title.en: Vayera: the first sprouting of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Vayera is the first place the Torah hints at Moshiach: Lot's daughters are called 'nimtza'os', as David is 'matzasi', and from Moav came Rus and from her Moshiach, hidden in a shameful origin. This suits Rosh Hashanah, whose tefillos ask for Hashem's kingship, and the reading ends with 'Maacha', hinted in sefarim to mean Melech al kol ha'aretz.

title.en: Kingdoms provoking each other: the Iran-Iraq war

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that when kingdoms provoke one another one should look out for Moshiach, and applies it to the war between Iran and Iraq, which statesmen fear could ignite the world. He cites a Pesikta in which the king of Persia provokes the king of Arabia, who goes to the king of Edom for counsel, and Hashem tells Israel not to fear. The leaders are only puppets; Hashem runs the world, and events are a call to teshuvah.

title.en: A gmar chasimah until Chanukah and on Hoshana Rabbah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Vayera is a renewed Rosh Hashanah, and cites the custom of the Ba'al Shem Tov's students to wish a gmar chasimah until the last day of Chanukah. He asks where this is written, and asks further about Hoshana Rabbah as a final sealing, which the Gemara does not mention: there is a hint in the Yerushalmi, it is explicit in the Ramban on Shelach, and its root is in the Zohar, which the Rambam did not have.

title.en: Revealed when the generation needs it: Hoshana Rabbah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that every prophecy, Malachi's too, was received at Sinai and revealed when its generation needed it. Earlier, greater generations did teshuvah in the Ten Days through fasting and afflictions, and one who wasted those days, like Naval, had no further mercy. Later, weaker generations in exile could not do this, so they were shown teshuvah through the joy of Sukkos, with Hoshana Rabbah as the final day.

title.en: Chanukah for the generation of ikvesa d'meshicha

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that from the Ba'al Shem Tov's time came the generations of ikvesa d'meshicha, souls so small that even love and joy cannot bring them to teshuvah. For them the sealing at Chanukah was revealed, as Rashi says the angels of mercy waited until evening before destroying Sedom; what is asked of them is a simple daily routine, living as a Jew according to the Shulchan Aruch.

title.en: Three months until Chanukah: the Bas Ayin and the Maharal

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bas Ayin on Vayeshev that during the three months Tishrei, Cheshvan and Kislev Klal Yisrael, likened to Tamar, waits for the sealing of Chanukah, and a hint from the Kedushas Levi on the thirty-six lights. From Vayera begin forty days, like the forty days of the Mabul that became forty days of Torah, ending at Chanukah, the third sealing after Yom Kippur and Hoshana Rabbah. With the Maharal's link of 25 Elul to 25 Kislev, he explains that the first quarter of the year is like infancy and does not yet count.

title.en: A person's first twenty years as his time until Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies this to a person's life: the first twenty years are his period until Chanukah, as the Noda BiYehudah wrote that tinokos shel beis rabban last until twenty. With the Lechovitcher on 'sa'adu libchem' he says a bochur in yeshivah must take provisions for the desert of life, building his mind, the sun, through Gemara and Tosafos, and his heart, the moon, through aggadah, hashkafah and tefillah. Sefer Bereishis likewise is the period of chinuch.

title.en: Sefer HaYashar and the Akeidah seen from afar

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one lives with Avraham through the parsha, since the Torah is a Torah of life. Sefer Bereishis is called Sefer HaYashar after the upright Avos, and what is missing today is that uprightness. The Akeidah test was 'he saw the place from afar': Avraham did not feel and had to go without feeling, which matches the last generation before Moshiach, numb like the heel; yet Hashem looks at us with the same eyes as at the Avos.

title.en: "Hashem yireh": serving in the dark

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'Hashem yireh': after the test Avraham established that Jews come three times a year to that place to be seen. In hester panim one serves with routine, and in the end Hashem reveals Himself to those who strive. He contrasts the blindness of the people of Sedom, and of today's world that sees the danger and does not do teshuvah, with Avraham, who did not let the darkness enter his soul, and closes with 'kach na', a request, and a wish for a gmar chasimah tovah until Chanukah.

catalogTitle: אליעזר's Change from ארור to ברוך The Jewish Instinct of. אמונה

oneLiner.en: From Eliezer's hidden wish that Yitzchak marry his own daughter, the Mashgiach shows how self-interest blinds a person, and explains that a Jew's emunah is an inborn instinct, inherited through the mother, that only sin and rationalization can dull.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Eliezer's mission to find a wife for Yitzchak and asks, following Rashi, why the word 'ulai' (perhaps) is written without a vav, readable as 'eilai' (to me), only when Eliezer retells the story. He answers that Eliezer, a great tzaddik, hoped Yitzchak would marry his own daughter, but this interest was hidden even from himself; only after Hashem showed him Rivka could he admit it. From here he returns to the question left open last time: if every Jew instinctively believes, why do some not? Besides spiritual sickness, people are blinded by their desires and rationalize, like the wolf and the sour grapes or theorists who invent how the world works rather than read the Creator's book. He distinguishes ta'avah from ga'avah, explains that a Jew's emunah is a feeling inherited from the mother, shown through the Maharal and Hebrew grammar, and closes by warning that philosophy cannot reach G-dliness.

en: A personal interest can be hidden even from the person himself; Eliezer could only recognize his wish for Yitzchak as a son-in-law after it could no longer come true.
Every Jew instinctively believes in Hashem as a descendant of Avraham Avinu; when a Jew does not believe, it is because his emunah is sick or because he is blinded by his own interests.
People reject the Torah's account of creation because the Torah also tells them what to do and not do, and accepting it would stand in the way of their pleasures.
Those driven by ta'avah often return when age takes their desires away, but those driven by ga'avah do not, since conceit grows with age.
A Jew's emunah is more emotion and instinct than intellect, and therefore it comes from the mother, which is why Jewishness follows the mother while tribe and inheritance follow the father.
Keeping the Torah keeps one's spiritual organism healthy and the instinctive emunah strong; one who strayed can be healed through the guidance of Torah sages.
Philosophy is not the way for us to reach G-dliness: the human mind was not made for it, and weighing both sides of the question of G-d's existence is itself dangerous.

candidateTopics: Eliezer and the shidduch of Yitzchak
Hebrew grammar and the word em

title.en: Eliezer's mission and his retelling

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews how Avraham sent Eliezer to Charan for a wife for Yitzchak, how Rivka came out exactly as Eliezer had prayed, and how the Torah repeats the whole story as Eliezer retold it to her family.

title.en: Ulai without a vav: Eliezer's hidden wish

summary.en: Following Rashi and the Sfas Emes, the Mashgiach asks why 'ulai' is written without a vav, readable as 'eilai', only in Eliezer's retelling. He explains that Eliezer, a great tzaddik who hoped his daughter would marry Yitzchak and was rejected as cursed, was blind to his own interest until Hashem showed him Rivka.

title.en: Why some Jews do not believe

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to last session's question: if every Jew instinctively believes, why are there Jews who do not? Besides a spiritual sickness that dulls the yearning for Hashem, he adds that a person is blinded by his interests, illustrated by the wolf who called the grapes sour.

title.en: Rationalizing against the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows how a person drawn to forbidden pleasures concludes that the Torah is not good rather than admit his weakness, like the student who blames the lighting or the man who blames the hammer. Although the whole world cries out that there is a Creator, people invent theories to avoid admitting it.

title.en: The watch, the bugs and the watchmaker's book

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the story he once told his fifth-grade class about two newcomers who theorized that bugs chasing cheese drive a watch, until told to read the watchmaker's book. Likewise, instead of theorizing how the world works, one should learn the book written by its Maker, the Chumash, with Rashi, Ramban and the Midrashim.

title.en: Why they reject the Creator's book

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that people would accept the Chumash if it ended with creation, but it also commands, so like Esav and Yishmael they reject it, a form of denial. This is why people who were not religious all their lives often turn to davening in old age, once their desires are gone.

title.en: Ta'avah and ga'avah; emunah as instinct

summary.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes people driven by ta'avah, who may do teshuvah when old, from those driven by ga'avah, which only grows, and ties this back to ulai and eilai. He then explains that beyond the intellectual proof any gentile can reach, a Jew has an inherited instinct that Hashem is his Father.

title.en: Three matzos, four cups: emunah from the mother

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal: the three matzos, from grain that brings knowledge, are the three Avos, and the four cups of wine, which stir emotion, are the four Imahos. Since a Jew's emunah is emotion more than intellect, it comes from the mother, which is why Jewishness follows the mother while tribe and inheritance follow the father.

title.en: Em from emunah: a rule of Hebrew grammar

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Lashon HaKodesh, the language of creation, holds clues to creation: a verb ending in nun drops it as a noun, as shanan gives shen, ganan gives gan and chanan gives chein. So aman, to believe, gives em, mother, while av, father, relates to wanting that comes from knowledge.

title.en: Believers, children of believers; keeping emunah healthy

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Moshe's worry that the Jews would not believe him and Hashem's answer that they are believers, children of believers, an instinct of the seed. He then explains that keeping the Torah keeps this instinct healthy, while sins sicken it until one is healed through the prescriptions of Torah sages.

title.en: Torah and mesorah, not philosophy

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the inborn emunah must be developed through learning Torah, and that the mesorah from Sinai is absolute proof, to be discussed later. Philosophy was used by great sages of earlier times against the influence of gentile writings in Spain and Arab lands, but it is alien to Torah and dangerous for us, since the mind was formed for this world, not for the abstract.

title.en: The wrong sense: a sixth sense and insulation

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares using the mind to grasp G-d to trying to see a symphony or hear a painting: no sharpening of the wrong sense will help. The sense for G-dliness is ruach hakodesh, which every Jew's neshamah has in potential, but sins insulate the mind from the neshamah like insulation on a wire; a tzaddik feels G-dliness to the degree of his righteousness.

title.en: The masterpiece and the danger of doubt

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chovos HaLevavos's mashal of a painting and poem that no spilled ink could produce: the world is a masterpiece showing its Maker, though the mind cannot grasp G-dliness itself. He explains why Ein Keloheinu precedes Mi Keloheinu, warns that weighing the possibility of no G-d is a departure from emunah, and closes that we hold to instinct, the evidence of creation and above all the mesorah.

catalogTitle: החוט הזהב של פרשת וירא הוא חסד

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains through the idea of gilgul why Avraham Avinu was moser nefesh for the people of Sodom, and then traces chesed as the golden thread that runs through all of parshas Vayeira.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why Avraham Avinu gave himself over for the people of Sodom. As an introduction he brings the Chasam Sofer on Yirmiyahu buying Chanamel's field: Yirmiyahu, a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, knew the churban came through him, and Hashem answered that a new body can still be a tzaddik. Following Rabbeinu Bachya, the people of Sodom were the dor haflagah and later the eidah of Korach; with the Rogatchover he shows how Tzoar, Admah and Tzevoim finished their judgment at Korach, and explains Lot's dwelling in a cave. From this he teaches that a believing Jew asks no questions on Hashem, since there are old accounts. Avraham davened for them because they were great souls. The second half follows chesed through the parsha: hachnasas orchim and the water brought through a messenger, Sodom's cruelty, Avimelech, and the akeidah, ending with the call to draw chesed from this Shabbos.

en: Yirmiyahu, a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, understood that the churban came through him, and Hashem answered him that his new body could still be a tzaddik.
The people of Sodom were gilgulim of the dor haflagah and came again as the eidah of Korach, where they completed their punishment.
A Jew who believes in gilgul does not ask questions on Hashem about suffering, since there are old accounts that only Hashem knows.
Every parsha has a thread running through it; in Lech Lecha it is emunah and in Vayeira it is chesed.
Avraham, who hated avodah zarah more than anyone, still hosted idol worshippers and had water brought by a messenger so as not to shame them.
Avraham's chesed was avodas Hashem and not a nature he could not overcome, as shown when he sent away Yishmael and went to the akeidah.
One can draw chesed from this parsha and Shabbos, which carries the power of Rosh Hashanah.

candidateTopics: the people of Sodom as the dor haflagah and Korach's eidah
chesed as the thread of parshas Vayeira

title.en: Yirmiyahu told to buy Chanamel's field

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens by asking why Avraham was moser nefesh for the people of Sodom, and as an introduction brings Yirmiyahu chapter 32: Hashem tells Yirmiyahu that his cousin Chanamel will come to sell him a field. The purchase was a sign that fields would again be bought in Eretz Yisrael after seventy years in Bavel, even as the Kasdim were about to take Yerushalayim.

title.en: Chanamel's plan and Yirmiyahu as Shlomo's gilgul

summary.en: Following the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach explains that Chanamel wanted to sell the body of the field and keep its fruits, thinking that nothing would happen to the fields of a tzaddik like Yirmiyahu. But Yirmiyahu knew he was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, whose marriage to Pharaoh's daughter on the night the Beis HaMikdash was finished brought the decree of churban, so he felt Chanamel was mocking him.

title.en: Yirmiyahu's tefillah and Hashem's answer

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Yirmiyahu's tefillah in this light: Hashem knows each person's earlier gilgul, and Yirmiyahu must see the churban he caused as Shlomo. Hashem answers 'I am the G-d of all flesh': the soul carries the old account, but the new body can still be a tzaddik, so Chanamel's sale is not foolish.

title.en: Sodom, the dor haflagah and Korach's eidah

summary.en: Bringing Rabbeinu Bachya, the Mashgiach explains that the people of Sodom were the dor haflagah reincarnated, and came again as the eidah of Korach. He shows hints for this: 'anshei ha'ir', 'anshei shem', the Targum's word for Korach's split, and their fear of being blinded; and he uses it to explain why Korach's small children were punished, citing the Ramban on Iyov.

title.en: Tzoar, Admah and Tzevoim finished at Korach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Targum Yonasan that the people of Bela, which is Tzoar, sank into the earth, and explains that they were swallowed with Korach to pay the old debt. He then brings the Rogatchover that Sodom was judged as an ir hanidachas, of which only two may be burned, and adds that Admah and Tzevoim received their burning in Korach's eidah, which was both swallowed and burned.

title.en: Why Lot dwelt in a cave

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah records that Lot dwelt in a cave. He brings the Gemara in Gittin about a widow's curse fulfilled literally and the Chasam Sofer, who left his city after a dream, and explains that Lot belonged under the decree of Sodom and fulfilled it by living as if buried, like the sukkah that stands in for galus.

title.en: No questions on Hashem: the old accounts

summary.en: The Mashgiach draws the lesson: a Jew who believes the Ramban and Rabbeinu Bachya on gilgul does not ask why a tzaddik suffers, and he rejects the books that question Hashem about the six million. He adds what the sefarim write about the gezeiros of tach, that those killed were gilgulim of those who opposed Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai, hinted in the large letters of the Megillah.

title.en: The thread of each parsha: Vayeira and chesed

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers his opening question: Avraham davened for Sodom because they were great souls who would yet come to their tikun. He then says every parsha has a thread from beginning to end; the parshiyos of the Avos, like the brachah of Avos in Shemoneh Esrei, require special kavanah, and while Lech Lecha's thread is emunah, Vayeira's is chesed.

title.en: Hachnasas orchim and the water through a messenger

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Avraham's hachnasas orchim for guests he thought were idol-worshipping Arabs, and brings the Satmar Rav's explanation of Avraham's 400 chapters of Avodah Zarah: his sensitivity to idolatry was far beyond ours. He asks why Avraham did everything himself but had water brought by a messenger, and answers that he did not want to shame the guests by washing their feet himself; he ties this to Moshe's water through a messenger and the Or HaChaim on why Moshe did not enter Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Sodom's cruelty and Avraham's tefillah for it

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Sodom as the exact opposite of Avraham: a city with a system of cruelty, where a girl who gave bread to a poor man was smeared with honey for the insects. Yet Avraham, their greatest opponent, davened for them and even spoke boldly to Hashem, 'chalilah lecha', which shows the greatness of his chesed.

title.en: Avimelech and 'when G-d made me wander'

summary.en: On Avraham's words to Avimelech, the Mashgiach brings the Targum Onkelos, which reads the verse as Hashem's chesed in bringing Avraham close while the world served idols, and the Lubliner Rav's explanation of why Onkelos, a convert, could feel this. Avraham always saw Hashem's chesed and in hard times would review it with Sarah; this is the chesed he asked of her.

title.en: Drawing chesed from the parsha; chesed and the akeidah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the whole parsha is full of chesed and carries the power of Rosh Hashanah, whose leinings are both in it. He shows that Avraham's chesed was avodas Hashem, since he rose early to send away Yishmael and to go to the akeidah, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar that at the akeidah Avraham took on Yitzchak's gevurah. He closes that every Jew was in Yitzchak on the akeidah, and asks to take the parsha's lesson of chesed for the whole year.

catalogTitle: מפרשיות של האבות אנו לומדים איך להתנהג

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that each of the Avos embodied one middah, that the nations descended from their 'waste' carry those middos in a corrupted form, and that the episode of Yishmael's expulsion is a sign of what will happen to his descendants' hold on Eretz Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by explaining that the Torah teaches the ways of the Avos before the mitzvos: Avraham is chesed, Yitzchak din, and Yaakov rachamim, a blend of the two. From Avraham's chesed came Yishmael, chesed gone bad, as seen in the Gemara that the Arabs took nine measures of immorality; from Yitzchak's din came Esav, the murderer. He traces how Jewish practice always leads with the right side, how the nations' writing, colors and calendars reflect din or unblended chesed, and why the Jewish calendar balances moon and sun. He then explains that Yitzchak never appears alone in the parshiyos, and that Sodom was condemned for combining cruelty with immorality. Turning to 'maaseh avos siman labanim', he explains that Yishmael's milah is empty, so the land he holds stays barren, and that Yishmael's expulsion after Yitzchak's milah foreshadows the future. He closes urging tefillah, Torah and chesed in a critical time.

en: Each of the Avos specialized in one middah: Avraham in chesed, Yitzchak in din, and Yaakov in rachamim, which is chesed blended with a measure of din.
Yishmael is the waste of Avraham's chesed and Esav the waste of Yitzchak's din, while Yaakov's blended middah produced no waste.
Jewish practice gives chesed, the right side, the lead while keeping some din, as in the order of washing, dressing, tefillin straps, writing and the leap year.
Yishmael's milah is an empty, imitation milah, so the Eretz Yisrael given to him in its merit remains barren and empty.
By 'maaseh avos siman labanim', Yishmael's expulsion right after Yitzchak's milah signals that when Yitzchak's covenant shines, Yishmael will lose his connection to Eretz Yisrael.
In a critical time of possible war, the Mashgiach says every Jew must strengthen himself in Torah, tefillah and chesed and pray that the geulah come with mercy.

the Jewish calendar and the leap year
war as the beginning of geulah

title.en: The middos of the three Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that before the mitzvos the Torah teaches how the Avos conducted themselves, and that each specialized in one middah: Avraham chesed, Yitzchak din, Yaakov rachamim as a blend of both. From Avraham's chesed came a waste product, Yishmael.

title.en: Chesed and din corrupted: Yishmael and Esav

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the Arabs took nine of ten measures of immorality and the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'chesed hu' as chesed misused. Esav is the waste of Yitzchak's din, and the Midrash shows Esav rejecting the Torah over 'do not murder' and Yishmael over 'do not commit adultery'.

title.en: Right before left: chesed leads

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows from the Shulchan Aruch that Jews always begin with the right side, the side of chesed, in washing, dressing and the tefillin straps. He contrasts Jewish writing from right to left with the nations, who follow their heavenly angel, and with Yishmael, and notes that even a sofer's letters mix in some din.

title.en: Red and white, sun and moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that all nations sense that red is din and white is chesed, citing the Shelah on white clothing on Yom Kippur. Esav's nations count by the red sun, Jews by the white moon while also reckoning with the sun through the leap year, and the Arabs by the moon alone, which is why Ramadan wanders through the seasons.

title.en: Esav's red, and Yitzchak never alone

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions the Shulchan Aruch's caution against red garments and Esav's attachment to red and to the reddish star Mars. He explains that learning each sidra with its meforshim awakens the chesed of the Avos, and notes that Yitzchak never has a sidra to himself but always appears together with Avraham or Yaakov.

title.en: The complaint against Sodom

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham's intense chesed aroused an accusation against Sodom. Reading 'ra'im v'chata'im laShem me'od', he explains that Sodom combined cruelty with immorality, two opposite extremes that leave no excuse, showing a deliberate rebellion against Hashem.

title.en: Maaseh avos siman labanim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban's principle that what happened to the Avos foreshadows their children, illustrated by Avraham's descent to Mitzrayim. He applies it to the seemingly small episode of Hagar and Yishmael in this week's parsha, which the Torah did not record merely as a story.

title.en: Yishmael's empty milah and the barren land

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the complaint of Yishmael's angel that his people also keep milah, and answers from the Rambam that milah weakens desire, so a nation steeped in immorality has an empty milah. Because Eretz Yisrael comes through milah, Yishmael received it, but empty; the land stayed barren under Arab rule and blooms with the Jews' return, and he links milah, 'Bereishis' as a covenant of fire, and the Arabs' control of oil.

title.en: Yishmael driven out; a call for this time

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Avraham's prayer for Yishmael with Yitzchak's true milah at eight days, after which Sarah has Yishmael driven out, a sign that when Yitzchak's covenant shines Yishmael will lose Eretz Yisrael. He then speaks of the threat of war, brings the Chasam Sofer and the Gemara that war is a beginning of geulah, and calls for Torah, tefillah and chesed.

catalogTitle: גודל נסיון של העקידה - "וירא את המקום מרחוק" - וזהו נסיון של דורנו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the greatness of the Akeidah test lay in serving Hashem through questions and hiddenness, 'vayar es hamakom merachok', and that this is the test of our generation, the 'heels' before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara's parable of the king who asked his general to fight one more war, and asks why the tenth test, the Akeidah, was the hardest: Avraham found Hashem on his own and suffered for it, and by now he was a prophet who would naturally obey. He answers that the test was one of questions: Hashem had promised 'ki b'Yitzchak yikarei lecha zera', yet Avraham went with closed eyes and with joy, not questioning, though a simple answer existed, because in a test one does not see the answer. 'Vayar es hamakom merachok': Hashem seemed far away and even his fervor was taken from him. Through the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, the Mashgiach applies this to the last generation, the heels of Adam's body, living in hiddenness and questions. He adds the story of Bar Daroma, then explains why Avraham's mesirus nefesh was unique: he gave up his own life's ideal. He closes with Kislev as a time for daily mesirus nefesh beyond habit.

en: The Akeidah, Avraham's tenth and hardest test, was a test of questions: Hashem's command seemed to contradict His promise that Avraham's line would come through Yitzchak.
Avraham went to the Akeidah with closed eyes and with joy, like a Jew saying Shema, refusing to entertain questions on Hashem.
'Vayar es hamakom merachok' means Hashem appeared distant to Avraham: hester panim, and even his fervor was taken from him.
By the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, the Akeidah foreshadows the last test of the Jewish people before Moshiach.
The last generation are the heels of Adam's body, who barely feel Hashem; holding on to emunah through this darkness is their task and will bring the geulah.
Avraham's mesirus nefesh at the Akeidah was unique because he sacrificed his own life's ideal, the people that would publicize Hashem's name.
Mesirus nefesh is not only giving one's life; every act for Hashem beyond one's habit is mesirus nefesh, and Kislev is its month.

title.en: The tenth test and the general's last war

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Akeidah is said every morning, brings the Gemara's parable of a king asking his victorious general to fight one more hard war, and asks why the last test should be the hardest when Avraham's first struggle, finding Hashem alone and standing up to Nimrod, seems far harder.

title.en: A prophet's test: the promise of Yitzchak

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a nisayon is meant to raise a person, like a child's test for promotion. Since Avraham was already a prophet who would obey any command, he finds the test in the contradiction to 'ki b'Yitzchak yikarei lecha zera', and brings that Avraham's praise was that he did not question Hashem's ways.

title.en: Closed eyes and 'vayar es hamakom merachok'

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the test of doubts: Avraham went with closed eyes, like saying Shema. He asks why Avraham did not see the simple answer Rashi brings, and answers that in a test one does not know the answer; 'vayar es hamakom merachok' means Hashem seemed far away, and Avraham went with joy, trusting the questions would melt.

title.en: Fervor taken away; the deeds of the fathers

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds that Hashem took away Avraham's fervor, yet he went with joy and mesirus nefesh. He then brings the Ramban's rule that what happened to the Avos is a sign for their children, with the examples of the famine, Egypt and Pharaoh, and concludes that the Akeidah's 'merachok' foreshadows the Jewish people's last test before Moshiach.

title.en: The heels of Adam: the generation before Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that all souls were in Adam's body: the generation of the desert was the head, and the last generation are the heels, which barely feel pain, Jews who do not feel Hashem amid hester panim and decades of questions. He brings Daniel's last chapter and the verses in Malachi about those who fear Hashem speaking to one another.

title.en: Emunah in the darkness brings the geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham passed the Akeidah in a state like the heels before Moshiach, and as a sign for the children, Jews who hold on to emunah will merit the geulah and sing 'merosh amanah'. Each generation has its own test; ours is emunah amid the minus and pritzus the Gemara foretold for the end of days.

title.en: Bar Daroma and today's heroes

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Gemara's story of Bar Daroma, the mighty warrior who said Hashem need not help, and explains that many Jews were killed because they relied on his strength. He applies it to today, when newspapers glorify leaders and generals, and says a Jew must cry out that Hashem alone runs the world, bringing the Midrash on Achashverosh and 'tzaddik be'emunaso yichyeh'.

title.en: What made Avraham's mesirus nefesh unique

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what is great in Avraham's mesirus nefesh when soldiers and idealists also give their lives, explains that people sacrifice themselves for honor, memory or an ideal, and that Avraham's ideal was to publicize Hashem's name, for which he asked for children. Through him mesirus nefesh became an inheritance of every Jew, whose soul is a part of Hashem.

title.en: Giving up his ideal; Kislev and daily mesirus nefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why even the lowest Jew gives his life, then shows that at the Akeidah Avraham gave up his life's ideal itself, proving his earlier sacrifices were not for an ideal. He brings Rashi on the dispute of Yitzchak and Yishmael, and closes with Kislev as the month of mesirus nefesh: doing more than one's habit in learning, tzedakah and davening, and a daily accounting.

catalogTitle: The Uniqueness of the שידוך of יצחק and רבקה שידוכים: Seeing Open השגחה פרטיות, Sublime Origin, Guidance - Meet בקדושה, We Need תפילה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that shidduchim are the one place where Hashem lets us glimpse His hidden hashgacha pratis, why an ordinary shidduch needs a 'lie' thrown to the Satan while the holy shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka did not, and why a bochur must guard himself and daven much for his zivug.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the first Ani Maamin and the Ba'al Shem Tov's falling leaf: every detail is guided by Hashem, but hidden. Shidduchim are the one area where He lets us see it, as the Midrash of Cleopatra shows. He asks why Rabbi Yaakov Emden wrote a jest about the shadchan and falsehood, and answers with the Tzemach Tzedek: a shidduch is so lofty that bringing it down needs some coarseness, a lie, and the shadchan is paid for the lie. That lie is the bone thrown to the Satan, like the se'ir la'azazel and the goat hairs on tefillin. The shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka was so holy it needed no lie, so Eliezer is not named. He urges the bochurim to guard themselves, to daven much, citing Moshe's 515 tefillos, and to say Lulei Hashem. He ends with Besuel, Lavan and Kislev.

en: Everything in the world, down to how a falling leaf lands, is guided by Hashem's individual hashgacha, but it is hidden from our eyes.
Shidduchim are the one area where Hashem shows His hand openly, and from there one can infer His control over everything else.
Following the Tzemach Tzedek, a shidduch is so lofty that bringing it into this world requires a lie, and the shadchan is paid for saying it.
The lie is what is thrown to the Satan so he does not spoil a great mitzvah, as with the se'ir la'azazel and the hairs on the tefillin.
The shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka was so holy that no lie was needed; Eliezer told only the truth.
One may need very many tefillos for a shidduch, as Moshe Rabbeinu needed one more than his 515, so one should keep davening and start early.

candidateTopics: the shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka

title.en: Hashgacha pratis is everywhere but hidden

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the first Ani Maamin and the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that how every falling leaf lands is decreed from Above. All this is hidden and looks natural; the one area where Hashem lets us glimpse it is shidduchim.

title.en: Cleopatra's challenge: Hashem makes matches

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Midrash of Cleopatra, who asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya what Hashem does since creation and failed when she paired a thousand slaves. He explains she thought the world runs by itself like a finished tape recorder, and that in shidduchim Hashem's hand is seen, as every couple has a story of wonders.

title.en: Rabbi Yaakov Emden's jest; a shidduch is hidden

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Rabbi Yaakov Emden, who surely shunned leitzanus, wrote a jest about shidduchim into a sefer. He brings Reb Velvel of Brisk that all the efforts are only for the nerves, and the Tzemach Tzedek that a shidduch is a hidden matter which even the malach announcing it does not know, like Shmuel who did not know which son of Yishai to anoint.

title.en: Why a shidduch needs a lie; paying the shadchan

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tzemach Tzedek that bringing so holy a thing down into this world needs some coarseness, so nearly every shidduch involves a lie of the shadchan. He tells of couples without shalom bayis whom a tzaddik told to pay the shadchan, and explains that one pays the shadchan for the lie, since Hashem does everything but will not lie.

title.en: Lulei Hashem ezrasa li; the parsha of shidduchim

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to Rabbi Yaakov Emden: the shadchan takes money for the lie. A shadchan may cause harm, but Hashem is the true help, as in the passuk 'Lulei Hashem ezrasa li', which Yaakov Avinu said going to Charan and which a sefer says to recite. He notes the minhag to read this parsha of Yitzchak and Rivka's shidduch from a second Sefer Torah for a chassan.

title.en: Guidance for bochurim; how shidduchim were made

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the bochurim to guard themselves from aveiros in their youth, which make the shidduch harder, and says meeting many times is unnecessary, since the Gemara only requires seeing her. He brings a German Rav on the parsha and Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky's account of his own brief meeting, and contrasts the old way, with fewer divorces, with American culture.

title.en: Eliezer's name; throwing a bone to the Satan

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Eliezer's name shows his mission was shidduchim, 'ezri me'im Hashem', and asks why his name is not mentioned in the whole parsha. He begins the answer: a shidduch needs a lie because the Satan must be thrown something, as with the se'ir la'azazel on Yom Kippur and the goat hairs that stick out of the tefillin.

title.en: The holy shidduch that needed no lie

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds the many mitzvos of a meal as another place something is given to the Satan, and says that in a shidduch he is given the sheker, his food. The shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka was Kodesh Kodashim, so no lie was needed; Eliezer told only the truth, acted only as Avraham's messenger, not as a shadchan, and therefore is not named.

title.en: A parsha of hashgacha; many tefillos needed

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the parsha a parsha of hashgacha pratis, touching in Eliezer's tefillah and thanks, and says one may need many tefillos for a shidduch. He brings Chazal that Moshe Rabbeinu davened 515 tefillos and one more would have brought him into Eretz Yisrael, urges the bochurim to start now saying the kapitel after Shemoneh Esrei as the Bnei Yissaschar says, and to stay pure in thought.

title.en: Besuel's poison and Lavan's fear

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Besuel poisoned Eliezer's food and a malach switched the dishes, and asks why Eliezer gave gifts to Rivka, her brother and mother but not to Besuel. He answers that Eliezer knew by ruach hakodesh what would happen and avoided any suspicion. He brings Targum Yonasan that Lavan is Bilam, and explains how Eliezer warned Lavan with 'vaHashem hitzliach darki'.

title.en: Shabbos Mevarchim Kislev

summary.en: The Mashgiach closes noting that this Shabbos is Shabbos Mevarchim Kislev, a month of light whose whole span is like a Yom Tov, when the Torah came out strong over the Lavans and Besuels in the days of the Chashmona'im. He calls for adding Torah and mitzvos and ends with a wish for the full light of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: ע"י קדושת ברית מילה זכה א"א למלכות - וזה מכוון למערת המכפלה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chevron and the Me'aras HaMachpela correspond to the mitzvah of milah, so that through holiness of the bris Avraham merited kingship there, and he applies this to every Jew's heart and to the search for a zivug.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that learning the parsha draws down its light. From the sefer Niflaos Hashem he brings that 'kings shall come from you' was said to Avraham in Chevron, where David was later crowned. He asks why Mamre, who advised Avraham about milah, is listed last, and builds on the Avnei Nezer's teaching that every place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a part of the Torah: Chevron and the Machpela correspond to milah, and one who guards the bris merits kingship. This explains Rashi's 'rising' of Efron's field from a commoner to a king, Avraham's discovery of the cave on the third day after his milah, and Efron as the orlah removed from that place. Every Jew has a Machpela in his heart once he removes the orlah of the heart. The Mashgiach then turns to Yitzchak's zivug: Eliezer's test with Lavan, prayer from youth, hishtadlus with bitachon, and the zivug as Hashem's own concern.

en: According to the Mashgiach, one who guards the holiness of the bris, in thought, speech, deed and sight, merits kingship for himself or for his children.
Chevron and the Me'aras HaMachpela correspond to the parsha and the halachos of milah, which is why kingship is tied to that place.
The Mashgiach teaches that every Jew has a Machpela in his heart, and when he removes the orlah of the heart his prayers can enter it and rise.
He says that one must begin praying for a zivug early and build up a reserve of prayers, since no one knows how many are needed.
According to the Mashgiach, a mitzvah requires hishtadlus done properly, together with bitachon, while the zivug itself is Hashem's own concern in which no one can interfere.
Eliezer went from cursed to blessed by setting aside his own interests and fully annulling himself to Avraham's will.

title.en: Chevron, kingship and the Machpela

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that learning the parsha draws down its light, then brings from the sefer Niflaos Hashem that 'kings shall come from you' was said to Avraham in Chevron, where David and Avshalom sought kingship. He describes the holiness of the Machpela, through which prayers and souls pass, and how Efron sensed only darkness there.

title.en: Mamre, Kiryas Sefer and the place of milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Mamre, who advised Avraham about milah, is always listed last, and brings the Avnei Nezer's explanation of Asniel ben Kenaz and Kiryas Sefer: each place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a part of the Torah. He concludes that Chevron and the Machpela correspond to milah, and that guarding the bris brings kingship, as with Yosef and Boaz.

title.en: Efron's field rises: from commoner to king

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Rashi stresses that Efron's field rose from a commoner to a king, and answers that the place was created for kingship through the bris; only when Avraham acquired it is he first called a king. He then explains that Avraham discovered the Machpela on the third day after his milah, as a gift for the mitzvah.

title.en: Efron as the orlah; Avraham's own mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mamre was the owner of the area connected to milah, while Efron, with his narrow eye, was its orlah, which Avraham cut away. Each tzaddik is bound to a particular mitzvah, and Avraham's is milah, so the only place he bought with money was the Machpela.

title.en: A Machpela in every Jew's heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that when holiness prevails even the other side agrees, as the sons of Ches did. He then says every Jew must live through this parsha: each has a Machpela in his heart, and by removing the orlah of the heart and guarding eyes, thoughts and mouth his prayers can enter it and he can become a king over himself.

title.en: Yitzchak's zivug and Eliezer's test

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects the search for Yitzchak's zivug to holiness of the bris, through Avraham's oath with 'place your hand under my thigh'. He then tells how Lavan, seeing the bracelets on Rivka, ran to Eliezer expecting him to have stumbled with his eyes, and found him standing firm in holiness.

title.en: Praying for a zivug from youth

summary.en: From Eliezer's prayer 'hakreh na lefanai hayom' the Mashgiach learns that even Avraham needed heavenly kindness for a zivug. He brings the Gemara in Berachos and the Bnei Yissaschar's advice, and urges starting young to build a reserve of prayers, as Moshe prayed 515 prayers and Avraham prayed for decades for a child.

title.en: Hishtadlus, bitachon and Hashem's business

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the water rose for Rivka the first time but not the second: a mitzvah requires effort. He says one must do the hishtadlus the Shulchan Aruch prescribes with bitachon, brings Adam who found his zivug in his sleep, and the question of the matron, concluding that matching couples is Hashem's own business in which no one can interfere.

title.en: Shlomo's daughter and the well

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Midrash of Shlomo HaMelech, who hid his daughter on an island to prevent the match he foresaw, and how a great bird carried her destined husband there. He then brings the Midrash that three found their zivug at a well, explaining that the well points to Hashem, the source of living waters.

title.en: Eliezer from cursed to blessed

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Eliezer, who hoped his own daughter would marry Yitzchak, still carried out his mission with complete devotion and prayer, setting aside his interests, and so left the category of cursed for blessed. He concludes that even one who feels his nature holds him back can subordinate his will to Hashem's and become blessed.

catalogTitle: מדות חסד וגבורה על דרך קדושה - וההיפוך

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the middos of chesed and din (gevurah) as they are in holiness, where chesed prevails over din and the two are always joined, and as they are in their reversal, the kelipos of Yishmael and Esav, building on the Avos and the events of Parshas Chayei Sarah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Avraham seeking a match for Yitzchak before himself, and links it to the Zohar's teaching that Avraham shares Hillel's root of chesed and Yitzchak Shammai's root of din. He defines chesed as outward, straight light and din as inward contraction, and explains why the world, created first with din, now runs on din joined to rachamim with chesed prevailing. Yishmael is the kelipah of chesed and Esav the kelipah of din; the Jews alone pair the two. From here he explains why Eretz Yisrael was held by Yishmael, the oil given to the Arabs, the right-to-left of Jewish writing, the man going first, and the seven Canaanite nations. He then asks why the angel of Sedom came to Avraham, teaches through the Chiddushei HaRim that a shaliach succeeds through bittul, explains Sarah's death and her 127 years, and closes by urging the use of the years of youth and the uprooting of the Yishmael within.

en: Avraham, like Hillel, draws from the root of chesed and Yitzchak, like Shammai, from the root of din; each person receives the Torah through the channel of his own root.
Chesed is outward expansion, straight light going from a person to another; din is contraction inward, and it shows itself as judging, as might or as fear.
Since the world could not stand with din alone, din must always be joined with chesed, and the avodah of a Jew is to make chesed prevail over din, right over left.
Yishmael is the kelipah of chesed and Esav the kelipah of din; each has one side alone, while the Jews hold both in holiness, joined as the two Names of Hashem are joined.

Yishmael's circumcision does not lessen his desire, which shows that the holiness of a Jew is in his very essence, and Eretz Yisrael was given to Yishmael to hold precisely because he has no share in the holiness of the bris.
A shaliach who fully nullifies his will to his sender carries the sender's strength with him, and every Jew is a shaliach of the Ribono shel Olam.
The years of youth are the time of chesed and love, and they must be used for the service of Hashem rather than slept away or spent on the kelipah of chesed.
